keyVerseText: And the sons of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son. Jeconiah: also called, Jehoiachin 2kin.24.6, Zedekiah: or Coniah ier.22.24
rootMeaning: The Hebrew name יְכׇנְיָה (Yᵉkonyâh) derives from the root כּוּן (kûwn), which conveys ideas of firmness, stability, and establishment, combined with יָהּ (Yah), a shortened form of the divine name Jehovah. Thus, the literal meaning is 'Jehovah will establish' or 'Yahweh establishes.' This etymology emphasizes God's sovereign action in establishing or confirming, adding a layer of divine assurance and faithfulness to the name beyond its common English transliteration as Jeconiah.
usageInScripture: The word יְכׇנְיָה appears seven times in Scripture, consistently translated primarily as 'Jeconiah,' referring to the Jewish king who reigned briefly before captivity. Variations such as 'of Jeconiah,' 'with Jeconiah,' and 'that Jeconiah' show its use mainly as a proper name tied closely to the historical figure. This consistent translation underlines its identity as a royal name rather than a common noun, anchoring it firmly in the narrative of Judah's monarchy and exile.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding יְכׇנְיָה as 'Jehovah will establish' highlights the paradox of God's sovereignty amid human failure and judgment. Jeconiah's short reign and subsequent exile illustrate God's disciplinary purposes, yet the name itself carries a promise of divine establishment. For the Christian faith, this points to God's ultimate control over history and kingship, foreshadowing the Messiah who truly establishes God's eternal kingdom. It reminds believers that even in apparent defeat or exile, God's plan for restoration and stability remains secure.
keyVerseReflection: 1 Chronicles 3:16 lists Jeconiah as the son of Jehoiakim and father of Zedekiah, also noting his alternate name Jehoiachin. This verse situates Jeconiah within the Davidic lineage, underscoring his role in the royal succession despite his troubled reign. The name יְכׇנְיָה here affirms God's enduring promise to establish His covenant people through this line, even as the historical narrative points to exile and judgment.
